44. // Use relaxed ordering for all atomic operations to mitigate synchronization overhead. It is safe
45. // to use this ordering semantics because Nanvix is a single-core system, and the kernel runs with
46. // interrupts disabled.
47. const ORDER: Ordering = Ordering::Relaxed;
48. 
49. //==================================================================================================
50. // Global Variables
51. //==================================================================================================
52. 
53. /// Physical memory manager storage.
54. static mut PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER: MaybeUninit<PhysMemoryManager> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
55. 
56. /// Whether the physical memory manager has been initialized.
57. static PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER_INIT: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);
58. 
59. //==================================================================================================
60. // Structures
61. //==================================================================================================
62. 
63. ///
64. /// # Description
65. ///
66. /// Physical memory manager.
67. ///
68. #[verus_verify]
69. pub struct PhysMemoryManager {
70.     upool: Upool,
71. }
72. 
73. //==================================================================================================
74. // Implementations
75. //==================================================================================================
76. 
77. impl PhysMemoryManager {
78.     ///
79.     /// # Description
80.     ///
81.     /// Initializes the physical memory manager singleton.
82.     ///
83.     /// # Parameters
84.     ///
85.     /// - `upool`: User page pool.
86.     ///
87.     /// # Errors
88.     ///
89.     /// Returns `InvalidArgument` if the singleton has already been initialized.
90.     ///
91.     // Trusted shim: writes the `static mut` singleton storage and an `AtomicBool`
92.     // lifecycle gate (raw global state Verus cannot model). The manager-singleton
93.     // lifecycle flag is distinct from the frame-allocator lifecycle and has no
94.     // abstract model (the do-not-modify `PhysMemView` only tracks the allocator);
95.     // the contract therefore states the caller-relevant guarantee: the global
96.     // frame allocator stays initialized and well-formed across this call.
97.     #[cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, allow(verus_impl_method_marker))]
98.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
99.     #[verus_spec(result =>
100.         requires
101.             phys_view().initialized,
102.             phys_view().inv(),
103.         ensures
104.             phys_view().inv(),
105.             phys_view().initialized,
106.     )]
107.     pub(super) fn init(upool: Upool) -> Result<(), Error> {
108.         if unlikely(PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
109.             return Err(Error::new(
110.                 ErrorCode::InvalidArgument,
111.                 "physical memory manager already initialized",
112.             ));
113.         }
114. 
115.         // SAFETY: this happens during kernel initialization and no other threads are running.
116.         unsafe { PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER.write(PhysMemoryManager { upool }) };
117.         PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER_INIT.store(true, ORDER);
118.         Ok(())
119.     }
120. 
121.     ///
122.     /// # Description
123.     ///
124.     /// Gets a mutable reference to the physical memory manager.
125.     ///
126.     /// # Panics
127.     ///
128.     /// Panics if the physical memory manager is not initialized.
129.     ///
130.     /// # Safety
131.     ///
132.     /// This function is unsafe because it returns a mutable reference to a global variable.
133.     ///
134.     /// The caller must ensure:
135.     ///
136.     /// - No other `&mut PhysMemoryManager` reference obtained from this function is live at the
137.     ///   same time (i.e., `&mut` references must not overlap). In practice this is guaranteed
138.     ///   because the kernel is single-threaded and runs with interrupts disabled, so no
139.     ///   re-entrant or concurrent call can alias the reference.
140.     ///
141.     pub unsafe fn get_mut<'a>() -> &'a mut PhysMemoryManager {
142.         if unlikely(!PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
143.             panic!("physical memory manager is not initialized");
144.         }
145. 
146.         // SAFETY: the physical memory manager has been initialized, so the value is valid.
147.         PHYS_MEMORY_MANAGER.assume_init_mut()
148.     }
149. 
150.     ///
151.     /// # Description
152.     ///
153.     /// Allocates user frames into caller-provided storage.
154.     ///
155.     /// The returned frames are not guaranteed to be physically contiguous.
156.     /// User allocations are gated by the kernel watermark: if fulfilling the request would
157.     /// leave fewer than `KERNEL_WATERMARK` free frames, the allocation is rejected.
158.     ///
159.     /// # Parameters
160.     ///
161.     /// - `count`: Number of frames to allocate.
162.     /// - `frames`: Mutable reference to a pre-allocated vector into which to store those
163.     ///   frames' addresses. It should have sufficient capacity for `count` entries.
164.     ///
165.     /// # Return Values
166.     ///
167.     /// Upon success, `Ok(())` is returned and `frames` is filled with `count` frames. Upon failure, an
168.     /// error is returned and any frames allocated by this call are dropped by truncating `frames`
169.     /// back to empty.
170.     ///
171.     // Trusted shim: loops over the global frame allocator (`Upool::alloc`) and the

199.         &mut self,
200.         count: usize,
201.         frames: &mut Vec<UserFrame>,
202.     ) -> Result<(), Error> {

204.             let reason: &str = "frames vector is not empty";
205.             error!("{reason}");
206.             return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, reason));

215.         if count == 0 {
216.             return Ok(());

219.         Self::check_user_watermark(count)?;
220. 
221.         for _ in 0..count {
222.             match self.upool.alloc() {
223.                 Ok(frame) => frames.push(frame),
224.                 Err(error) => {
225.                     frames.clear();
226.                     return Err(error);

276.     /// watermark, i.e. that would drop the number of free frames below
277.     /// [`config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK`].
278.     ///
279.     /// # Parameters
280.     ///
281.     /// - `count`: Number of user frames the caller intends to allocate.
282.     ///
283.     /// # Returns
284.     ///
285.     /// Upon success, `Ok(())` is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
286.     ///
287.     // Trusted shim: reads the global free-frame count and compares it against
288.     // `KERNEL_WATERMARK + count`. Pure gate, no allocator state change. `Ok` exactly
289.     // captures the watermark policy: at least `KERNEL_WATERMARK` frames remain free
290.     // after servicing `count`. `Err` covers both the overflow guard and a breach.
291.     #[cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, allow(verus_impl_method_marker))]

293.     #[verus_spec(result =>
294.         requires
295.             phys_view().initialized,
296.             phys_view().inv(),
297.         ensures
298.             phys_view().inv(),
299.             phys_view().initialized,
300.             phys_view().frames.free_frames.finite(),
301.             match result {
302.                 Ok(()) => spec_watermark_ok(phys_view().frames, count as int),
303.                 Err(_) => true,
304.             },

306.     fn check_user_watermark(count: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
307.         let watermark_threshold: usize = config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK
308.             .checked_add(count)
309.             .ok_or_else(|| {
310.                 let reason: &str = "watermark + count overflow";
311.                 error!("{reason}");
312.                 Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, reason)
313.             })?;
314.         if frame::free_count() < watermark_threshold {
315.             let reason: &str = "would breach kernel watermark";
316.             error!("{reason}");
317.             return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::OutOfMemory, reason));
318.         }
319.         Ok(())
320.     }

323.     /// # Description
324.     ///
325.     /// Allocates a kernel frame.
326.     ///
327.     /// Kernel allocations bypass the watermark — no artificial ceiling.
328.     ///
329.     /// # Return Values
330.     ///
331.     /// Upon success, a kernel frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
332.     ///
333.     // Trusted shim: allocates one frame from the global allocator (bypassing the
334.     // watermark) and wraps it, freeing the raw frame if wrapping fails. On success
335.     // the returned frame's base address is now allocated and page-aligned.
336.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
337.     #[verus_spec(result =>
338.         requires
339.             phys_view().initialized,
340.             phys_view().inv(),
341.         ensures
342.             phys_view().inv(),
343.             phys_view().initialized,
344.             match result {
345.                 Ok(frame) => {
346.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(frame@)
347.                     &&& frame@ % spec_page_size() == 0
348.                 },
349.                 Err(_) => true,
350.             },
351.     )]
352.     pub fn alloc_kernel_frame(&mut self) -> Result<KernelFrame, Error> {
353.         let frame_addr: FrameAddress = frame::alloc()?;
354.         KernelFrame::new(frame_addr).inspect_err(|e| {
355.             warn!("failed to wrap frame after KernelFrame::new failure: {e:?}");
356.             if let Err(free_err) = frame::free(frame_addr) {
357.                 warn!("failed to free frame after KernelFrame::new failure: {free_err:?}");
358.             }
359.         })
360.     }
361. 
362.     ///
363.     /// # Description
364.     ///
365.     /// Allocates a contiguous range of kernel frames into caller-provided storage.
366.     ///
367.     /// Kernel stacks require physically contiguous frames because the kernel uses identity
368.     /// mapping and the hardware stack pointer traverses the region linearly.
369.     /// Kernel allocations bypass the watermark — no artificial ceiling.
370.     ///
371.     /// # Parameters
372.     ///
373.     /// - `count`: Number of frames to allocate.
374.     /// - `frames`: Mutable reference to a pre-allocated vector into which to store
375.     ///   those frames' addresses.
376.     ///
377.     /// # Return Values
378.     ///
379.     /// Upon success, `Ok(())` is returned and `frames` is filled with `count`
380.     /// contiguous entries. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
381.     ///
382.     // Trusted shim: allocates a physically-contiguous run from the global allocator
383.     // (bypassing the watermark) and wraps each frame, with a two-phase
384.     // (`Vec::clear` + `frame::free`) rollback Verus cannot body-verify without
385.     // editing exec code. On success exactly `count` frames are handed out, each now
386.     // allocated, and their base addresses form an ascending page-stride run
387.     // (contiguity is load-bearing for kernel stacks). On error the vector is emptied.
388.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
389.     #[verus_spec(result =>
390.         requires
391.             phys_view().initialized,
392.             phys_view().inv(),
393.             old(frames)@.len() == 0,
394.         ensures
395.             phys_view().inv(),
396.             phys_view().initialized,
397.             match result {
398.                 Ok(()) => {
399.                     &&& final(frames)@.len() == count
400.                     &&& forall|i: int|
401.                         0 <= i < count as int ==>
402.                             #[trigger] phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(final(frames)@[i]@)
403.                     &&& exists|base: int|
404.                         #[trigger] kernel_frames_contiguous(final(frames)@, base)
405.                 },
406.                 Err(_) => final(frames)@.len() == 0,
407.             },
408.     )]
409.     pub fn alloc_many_kernel_frames(
410.         &mut self,
411.         count: usize,
412.         frames: &mut Vec<KernelFrame>,
413.     ) -> Result<(), Error> {
414.         // Check if caller-provided vector is not empty.
415.         if !frames.is_empty() {
416.             let reason: &str = "frames vector is not empty";
417.             error!("{reason}");
418.             return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, reason));
419.         }
420.         if frames.capacity() < count {
421.             let reason: &str = "frames vector has insufficient capacity";
422.             error!("{reason}");
423.             return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, reason));
424.         }
425. 
426.         let base_addr: FrameAddress = frame::alloc_contiguous(count)?;
427.         let base_raw: usize = base_addr.into_raw_value();
428.         for i in 0..count {
429.             let raw_addr: usize = base_raw + i * mem::PAGE_SIZE;
430.             match FrameAddress::from_raw_value(raw_addr).and_then(KernelFrame::new) {
431.                 Ok(kf) => frames.push(kf),
432.                 Err(e) => {
433.                     // Drop already-wrapped frames (frees them via KernelFrame::Drop).
434.                     frames.clear();
435.                     // Free remaining un-wrapped frames from the contiguous allocation.
436.                     for j in i..count {
437.                         let leak_raw: usize = base_raw + j * mem::PAGE_SIZE;
438.                         if let Ok(fa) = FrameAddress::from_raw_value(leak_raw) {
439.                             if let Err(e) = frame::free(fa) {
440.                                 warn!("failed to free leaked frame {fa:?}: {e:?}");
441.                             }
442.                         }
443.                     }
444.                     return Err(e);
445.                 },
446.             }
447.         }
448.         Ok(())
449.     }
450. }

4. // PhysMemoryManager - Specifications
5. //
6. // `PhysMemoryManager` is a *stateless* facade over the global frame allocator
7. // (`Upool` carries no fields; kernel frames are drawn directly from `frame::*`).
8. // It therefore has no per-instance abstract state of its own: the caller-relevant
9. // state is the global frame-reservation state, modelled by the do-not-modify
10. // `phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView` in `mod.spec.rs`. All manager contracts are
11. // stated over `phys_view()` and the returned frame values -- exactly the monotone
12. // style used by the `frame::*` free-function shims (`book`, `alloc_range`, ...).
13. //
14. // See `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-manager/view_design.md` for why a bespoke
15. // `self@` View is *not* realizable here (a constant view cannot witness global
16. // mutation, and there is no `old(phys_view())`).
17. 
18. verus! {
19. 
20. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
21. use crate::mm::phys::{
22.     phys_view,
23.     FrameAllocView,
24. };
25. use vstd::seq::Seq;
26. 
27. /// The kernel watermark threshold, lifted to `int`.
28. ///
29. /// Abstract (uninterpreted) form of the build-time constant
30. /// `config::kernel::KERNEL_WATERMARK`: the number of physical frames the
31. /// allocator must keep in reserve for kernel use, below which user allocations
32. /// are refused. It is left opaque because the concrete value is a build-time
33. /// constant of an external crate; callers only rely on its consistency, not its
34. /// magnitude.
35. pub uninterp spec fn spec_kernel_watermark() -> int;
36. 
37. /// A user allocation of `count` frames is admissible only if, after servicing it,
38. /// at least `KERNEL_WATERMARK` frames would still be free.
39. ///
40. /// Stated on the abstract free-set cardinality -- never on an allocator counter --
41. /// so it survives any frame-allocator reimplementation. `free_frames.len()` is
42. /// meaningful because the allocator keeps `free_frames` finite (see the shim
43. /// contracts, which (re)establish `phys_view().frames.free_frames.finite()`).
44. pub open spec fn spec_watermark_ok(v: FrameAllocView, count: int) -> bool {
45.     v.free_frames.len() >= spec_kernel_watermark() + count
46. }
47. 
48. /// `addrs` is an ascending, page-stride-contiguous run of frame addresses based
49. /// at `base`: `addrs[i] == base + i * PAGE_SIZE`.
50. ///
51. /// Used to state the contiguity guarantee of `alloc_many_kernel_frames` over the
52. /// sequence of returned kernel-frame addresses (kernel stacks require a linear,
53. /// identity-mapped physical region).
54. pub open spec fn is_contiguous_run(addrs: Seq<int>, base: int) -> bool {
55.     forall|i: int|
56.         0 <= i < addrs.len() ==> #[trigger] addrs[i] == base + i * spec_page_size()
57. }
58. 
59. /// `frames` is an ascending, page-stride-contiguous run of kernel frames based at
60. /// `base`: the address of the `i`-th frame is `base + i * PAGE_SIZE`.
61. ///
62. /// Phrased directly over the `KernelFrame` sequence (using each frame's abstract
63. /// address `@`) so that the `alloc_many_kernel_frames` contiguity guarantee can be
64. /// triggered without an inline closure (closures are forbidden inside triggers).
65. pub open spec fn kernel_frames_contiguous(frames: Seq<KernelFrame>, base: int) -> bool {
66.     forall|i: int|
67.         0 <= i < frames.len() ==> #[trigger] frames[i]@ == base + i * spec_page_size()
68. }
69. 
70. } // verus!

5. //
6. // Abstract laws backing the caller-facing guarantees of the `PhysMemoryManager`

11. 
12. /// The many-frame watermark gate subsumes the single-frame one: if servicing
13. /// `count >= 1` frames still respects the watermark, then so does servicing one.
14. ///
15. /// Justifies that `alloc_user_frame` (count = 1) and `alloc_many_user_frames`
16. /// (count) share the same `check_user_watermark` policy.
17. pub proof fn lemma_watermark_monotone(v: FrameAllocView, count: int)
18.     requires
19.         count >= 1,
20.         spec_watermark_ok(v, count),
21.     ensures
22.         spec_watermark_ok(v, 1),
23. {
24. }
25. 
26. /// A contiguous run with a positive page stride has pairwise-distinct addresses:
27. /// distinct indices map to distinct frame addresses.
28. ///
29. /// Backs the "no double-allocation" reading of the contiguity guarantee in
30. /// `alloc_many_kernel_frames`: the `count` returned frames are genuinely distinct
31. /// physical frames, not aliases.
32. pub proof fn lemma_contiguous_run_distinct(addrs: Seq<int>, base: int)
33.     requires
34.         spec_page_size() > 0,
35.         is_contiguous_run(addrs, base),
36.     ensures
37.         forall|i: int, j: int|
38.             0 <= i < addrs.len() && 0 <= j < addrs.len() && i != j ==> addrs[i] != addrs[j],
39. {
40.     let ps = spec_page_size();
41.     assert forall|i: int, j: int|
42.         0 <= i < addrs.len() && 0 <= j < addrs.len() && i != j implies addrs[i]
43.         != addrs[j] by {
44.         assert(addrs[i] == base + i * ps);
45.         assert(addrs[j] == base + j * ps);
46.         if addrs[i] == addrs[j] {
47.             // From the equal addresses: i * ps == j * ps.
48.             vstd::arithmetic::mul::lemma_mul_is_commutative(i, ps);
49.             vstd::arithmetic::mul::lemma_mul_is_commutative(j, ps);
50.             // ps * (i - j) == ps * i - ps * j == 0.
51.             vstd::arithmetic::mul::lemma_mul_is_distributive_sub(ps, i, j);
52.             assert(ps * (i - j) == 0);
53.             // A nonzero stride times a nonzero difference cannot be zero.
54.             vstd::arithmetic::mul::lemma_mul_nonzero(ps, i - j);
55.             assert(false);
56.         }
57.     }
58. }
59. 
60. } // verus!

name: ast-consistency
description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
---

# AST Consistency Check

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |

description: "Detect spec weakening via tree-sitter comparison against a baseline SHA. Use in specification, proving, and cheating-elimination phases to enforce that requires/ensures are never silently removed or relaxed."

# Spec Drift Check

## What Is Spec Drift?

Spec drift occurs when a function's `requires` or `ensures` clauses are removed,
relaxed, or replaced with weaker versions during a pipeline phase. This is a
critical integrity violation because:

- **Callers depend on the spec.** Upstream modules may have already proven their
  correctness assuming the original spec. Weakening it silently breaks those proofs.
- **Weakening is never acceptable as a proof strategy.** If a spec is hard to
  prove, the proof needs strengthening, not the spec weakening.

## When to Use

Use this skill in **every review** during these phases:
- **Specification** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD
- **Proving** — compare specification END → current HEAD
- **Cheating Elimination** — compare phase START baseline → current HEAD

## How to Run

### Auto-detect mode (recommended)

The `check` subcommand reads `pipeline_state.json` to automatically determine
the module, source file, current phase, and baseline SHA:

```bash
python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check <module_name>
```

### Manual mode

Use `git-diff` when you need explicit control over the comparison range:

```bash
python3 scripts/spec_drift.py git-diff <source_file> --before <baseline_sha> [--after <ref>]
```

Where:
- `<source_file>` is the module's source file (relative to repo root)
- `<baseline_sha>` is the phase start SHA
- `--after` defaults to working tree if omitted

### Exit Codes
- **0** — No contract drift detected ✅
- **1** — Contract drift detected ⚠ — spec weakening found
- **2** — Fatal error (tool failure)

### Example

```bash
# Auto-detect from pipeline state
python3 scripts/spec_drift.py check libhfs-src-internal-volume_impl

# Build Nanvix

Use this skill when the user asks to build, compile, format, lint, or spell-check Nanvix. This
covers all build-system operations exposed through the `z` utility.

## Prerequisites

- Development environment set up per `doc/setup.md`.
- A local cross-compilation toolchain (`toolchain/`).
- **Windows 11:** GNU Make on PATH, Windows Hypervisor Platform enabled,
  Developer Mode enabled, and Rust toolchain installed. See `doc/setup.md` for details.

## Windows Setup Summary

Before building on Windows, ensure:

1. **Windows Hypervisor Platform** is enabled (`Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform -All`, then reboot).
2. **Developer Mode** is on (Settings > Privacy & Security > For developers).
3. **GNU Make** is on PATH (`winget install ezwinports.make`).
4. **Rust toolchain** is installed via `winget install Rustlang.Rustup`.
5. Repository was cloned with `git clone -c core.symlinks=true`.
6. Git hooks are installed: `./z.ps1 setup`.

## Building

### Preferred Build Commands (using `z` utility)

```bash
# Build everything with the local toolchain.
./z build -- all
```

### Building Individual Components

```bash
# Kernel only.
./z build -- kernel
# Nanvixd only.
./z build -- all-nanvixd
# UserVM only.
./z build -- all-uservm
```

### Build Parameters

Set these as environment variables or pass them after `--` in the `z` command:

| Parameter        | Values                   | Default         |
|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| `MACHINE`        | `microvm`                | `microvm`       |
| `TARGET`         | `x86`                    | `x86`           |
| `RELEASE`        | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `LOG_LEVEL`      | `trace`, `debug`,        | `error`         |
|                  | `info`, `warn`,          |                 |
|                  | `error`, `panic`         |                 |
| `PROFILER`       | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `DEPLOYMENT_MODE`| `standalone`,            | `standalone`    |
|                  | `single-process`,        |                 |
|                  | `multi-process`, `l2`    |                 |

Example with custom parameters:

```bash
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=error
```

### Manual Build Variants

```bash
# Default debug build.
./z build -- all
# Release build.
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=panic
# For echo-breakdown benchmark.
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=panic TIMESTAMP_MSG=yes
```

### Building on Windows (using `z.ps1`)

On Windows 11, the `z.ps1` PowerShell script provides the same CLI interface. Guest components are
cross-compiled using a local toolchain; host binaries (`nanvixd`, `uservm`) are built natively with the
microvm backend (WHP on Windows).

```powershell
# Build everything (guest via make + host binaries natively).
.\z.ps1 build -- all

# Build only the UserVM (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- uservm

# Build only nanvixd (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- nanvixd

# Build only nanvix-bench (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- nanvix-bench

# Build only guest components (kernel + hello-rust-nostd).
.\z.ps1 build -- guest

# Release build.
.\z.ps1 build -- all RELEASE=yes
```

Any unrecognized target is forwarded to `make`, just like on Linux:

```powershell
.\z.ps1 build -- kernel
.\z.ps1 build -- format-check
.\z.ps1 build -- lint-check
```

## Code Quality

### Formatting

```bash
# Check formatting issues.
./z build -- format-check
# Auto-fix formatting issues.
./z build -- format
```

### Linting

```bash
# Check linting issues.
./z build -- lint-check
# Auto-fix linting issues.
./z build -- lint
```

### Spell Checking

```bash
# Check spelling errors.
./z build -- spellcheck
# Fix spelling errors.
./z build -- spellcheck-fix
```

## Formal Verification

Nanvix uses Verus for formal verification of selected kernel crates. The expected Verus version is pinned in `build/verus-version`. Verification requires `VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR` to be set; when unset, `make verify` is a no-op.

```bash
# Install verus and run verification.
./scripts/setup/verus.sh ~/toolchain/verus
./z build -- verify VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR=~/toolchain/verus

# Verify a single crate.
./z build -- verify-bitmap VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR=~/toolchain/verus
```

- Set `VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR` to the directory containing the `verus` binary.
- Use `scripts/setup/verus.sh <dir>` to download the pinned release.
- The `vstd` crate version in `Cargo.toml` is exact-pinned (`=`) to match the Verus binary.

## Cleaning

```bash
./z clean        # Clean build artifacts.
./z distclean    # Remove all generated files.
```

### Cleaning on Windows

```powershell
.\z.ps1 clean        # Quick clean (UserVM artifacts + cache).
.\z.ps1 distclean    # Full clean (cargo clean + all artifacts).
```

## CI/CD Pipeline

```bash
# Run the full CI pipeline locally.
./scripts/pipeline.sh
```

The pipeline covers: spell checking, formatting, linting, building, and testing across multiple
machine and deployment configurations.

## IDE Setup (Optional)

### Visual Studio Code

Use the host-specific settings template. The Linux template invokes `./z`, while the Windows
template routes Rust Analyzer through `./z.bat build -- check`, which runs native `cargo check`
on host crates (`uservm`, `nanvixd`, `nanvix-test`, `mkramfs`).

**Linux:**

```bash
mkdir -p .vscode && cd .vscode
ln -s ../scripts/setup/vscode/settings-linux.json settings.json
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .vscode -Force
Copy-Item scripts\setup\vscode\settings-windows.json .vscode\settings.json
```

> **Note:** The `check` target in `z.ps1` only checks host crates natively. Guest and kernel
> crates require the cross-compilation toolchain. Run
> `.\z.ps1 build -- check-kernel check-guest-binaries` for a full cross-target check.

## Troubleshooting Build Issues

- If builds fail with toolchain errors, verify `toolchain/` symlink points to a valid toolchain.
- Use `./z help` for usage information.
- **Windows:** Use `.\z.ps1 help` for Windows-specific usage information.
- **Windows:** If the UserVM build fails, verify that the Windows Hypervisor Platform feature is
  enabled (`Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform`).
